Trying to Conceive

Fresh or frozen embryo transfer: choosing a strategy

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Fresh and frozen embryo transfers can both lead to a baby. The decision is whether transferring now or waiting offers a useful advantage for your particular treatment cycle. Ovarian response, embryo availability, the uterine lining and the reason for any testing can change that balance. A higher headline success rate for one method does not settle the choice for everyone.

Three choices are often confused

A fresh transfer places an embryo from the current egg-collection cycle into the uterus without first freezing it. A frozen embryo transfer uses a previously stored embryo after warming and assessment. Freeze-all means deliberately postponing the first transfer and storing the suitable embryos from that collection. These are related choices, but they are not interchangeable.

Having a fresh transfer does not mean discarding every other embryo. Suitable remaining embryos can be stored for another attempt or a future sibling. The useful comparison is therefore often a fresh-first strategy with later frozen transfers versus freezing all suitable embryos before any transfer. Ask which comparison your clinic means when it describes its success rate.

Start with the outcome and the denominator

An implantation rate, a positive pregnancy test and a live-birth rate answer different questions. A rate per embryo transferred also leaves out people who never reached transfer. Cumulative live birth follows the opportunity from a collection through subsequent transfers over a stated period. It can be more informative for choosing a strategy than the result of the first transfer alone.

Clinic figures may involve different ages, diagnoses, embryo stages and selection methods. A frozen-transfer group may contain embryos already selected for storage and survival after warming. That makes a simple comparison with all fresh cycles potentially misleading. Ask for results in patients with circumstances like yours, the number included, the time period and whether cancelled cycles are counted. A percentage is an estimate, not a personal promise.

PCOS and a strong ovarian response can change the balance

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, or OHSS, is a potentially serious response to ovarian stimulation. ASRM recommends considering a freeze-only cycle with later frozen transfer when a high ovarian response or elevated estradiol creates substantial risk. Avoiding pregnancy immediately after stimulation can reduce moderate or severe OHSS. The trigger medicine and the rest of the prevention plan also matter; freezing alone does not eliminate every early case.

A 2016 randomized trial involving 1,508 women with polycystic ovary syndrome found more live births after the first frozen transfer than after fresh transfer, about 49% versus 42%. OHSS was less common, but pre-eclampsia was more common after frozen transfer. This supports an individualized discussion in PCOS, not a rule that every person with that diagnosis (or every IVF patient) will do better with freezing. The study used up to two day-three embryos, which also limits direct comparison with other protocols.

Trials in other groups have not given one universal answer

A 2019 trial in 1,650 ovulatory women with a good prognosis found a higher singleton live-birth rate after frozen single-blastocyst transfer than after fresh transfer, about 50% versus 40%. Pre-eclampsia was also more frequent in the frozen group. In contrast, a 2020 European trial of women with regular cycles did not find a clear improvement in ongoing pregnancy or live birth with freeze-all, and pregnancy took longer to achieve. Its fresh-transfer strategy allowed postponement when safety concerns arose.

Follow-up of that same European trial, published in print in 2025, found similar cumulative live-birth rates after including later transfers from the collection: about 43% with freeze-all and 42% with the fresh-first strategy. The UK E-Freeze trial also did not demonstrate a higher healthy-baby rate from routine freezing, although recruitment below target and treatment crossover limited its certainty. Differences between populations and protocols are reasons to examine applicability, not to select whichever headline is most reassuring.

Fewer eggs or reduced ovarian reserve need particular attention

A 2025 randomized trial studied 838 women with a low IVF prognosis, defined by a low number of eggs retrieved or poor ovarian reserve. Live birth after the first transfer occurred in about 32% of the frozen group and 40% of the fresh group. Cumulative live birth within one year was also lower with the frozen strategy, about 44% versus 51%. These findings challenge the assumption that freezing all embryos is harmless to the chance of success in every patient group.

The results do not mean that a frozen embryo cannot lead to a baby when only a few eggs were obtained. Nor do they remove a medical reason to postpone transfer. They do mean that a clinic should explain why freeze-all is expected to help in your particular circumstances. Discuss the number of available embryos, safety concerns and realistic alternatives before accepting routine freezing as an automatic improvement.

The uterine lining and the preparation regimen matter

A clinic may postpone transfer to address the uterine lining or another treatment concern. For a later frozen transfer, some people can use an ovulation-based cycle; others need a programmed regimen with hormones to prepare the lining. A modified natural cycle may still involve a trigger injection or progesterone. Frozen transfer therefore does not always reproduce an entirely natural, medicine-free cycle.

A 2026 randomized trial of 4,376 ovulatory women planning a frozen single-blastocyst transfer found similar healthy live-birth rates with natural-ovulation and programmed preparation. Pre-eclampsia among clinical pregnancies was lower with natural preparation, about 3% versus 5%, but cycle cancellation was more frequent. This compared two ways of preparing for a frozen transfer, not frozen versus fresh transfer. It cannot establish the best regimen for someone who does not ovulate regularly.

Age and embryo grading require the right context

For the embryo’s age-related reproductive potential, ask about the age of the person providing the eggs when those eggs were collected. If donor eggs were used, that is the relevant egg-age history; the sperm donor’s age is not a substitute for it. The health and circumstances of the person carrying the pregnancy still need assessment when transfer is planned. Freezing does not turn an embryo into a guarantee of future fertility.

An embryologist assesses development and appearance to help rank embryos, but a grade does not establish every aspect of genetic health or promise implantation. Numbers such as 79%, 64% or 28% cannot be applied to a grade without knowing the study population, grading system and outcome measured. Ask what your own laboratory’s terminology means and how much uncertainty remains. A birthday threshold alone should not decide the transfer strategy.

Freezing can support future plans without guaranteeing them

Stored embryos can allow another attempt without repeating egg collection. They can also be part of fertility preservation before a treatment that may damage fertility, including some cancer treatment. If that is relevant, ask for timely coordination between the treating specialist and fertility team; do not delay necessary treatment on your own. Egg freezing and embryo freezing are different options because embryos have already been fertilized.

Modern freezing commonly uses vitrification, a rapid process designed to limit ice-crystal damage. Most embryos survive warming, but some do not, and occasionally no embryo is suitable for transfer. Discuss that contingency before the appointment. Ask about storage costs, consent and future-use arrangements, since rules differ between settings. Neither successful storage nor a long storage period proves that a healthy pregnancy will result.

Genetic testing is a separate decision

Embryos may be frozen while testing is completed, but the reason for the test matters. Testing for a particular inherited condition is different from PGT-A, which assesses chromosome number in sampled cells. PGT-A is a selection process, not a treatment that repairs an embryo. It can reduce the number available for transfer, and biopsy or an incorrect or uncertain result can affect the options.

HFEA does not find evidence that routine PGT-A improves the chance of a baby for most IVF patients. A possible reduction in miscarriage does not necessarily produce a higher overall live-birth rate. Ask which test is proposed, what it can and cannot detect, and whether its expected benefit applies to you. Freezing and testing should not be presented together as a guarantee of a healthy child.

Compare total cost, time and treatment burden

A transfer using embryos already stored may avoid the cost and physical demands of another stimulation and collection. That is different from saying freeze-all is cheaper than a fresh-first strategy. Freezing, storage, warming, monitoring and medicines can add costs. In the UK E-Freeze trial, routine freezing was more costly in that health-service setting; prices and funding elsewhere may differ.

Ask for an itemized estimate for each realistic plan, including what happens if a cycle is cancelled or an embryo does not survive warming. Delaying transfer can allow recovery or resolve a clinical concern, but it also adds waiting and appointments. Some people value time to prepare; others find the delay difficult. Neither reaction determines treatment success. A useful plan explains the medical reason, the likely timetable and the support available if it changes.

Leave with a reasoned plan and clear safety advice

Ask the team to state its main reason for recommending fresh transfer or postponement: OHSS prevention, a lining concern, testing, fertility preservation or an expected reproductive benefit in your patient group. Ask which evidence supports that benefit and whether it concerns the first transfer or the whole collection. The number of embryos transferred is a separate decision; high estrogen is not a reason by itself to transfer several embryos.

Follow your own medicine and monitoring instructions. Contact the fertility clinic as soon as possible for abdominal pain and bloating, vomiting, faintness or bleeding. Seek emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest or upper-back pain, marked thirst with reduced urine, swelling, lower abdominal pain on one side or shoulder-tip pain. These can signal serious OHSS or ectopic pregnancy. Do not wait for a scheduled transfer or pregnancy test to seek help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Randomized trials show that the balance differs by patient group. PCOS, good-prognosis ovulatory populations and low-prognosis populations should not be treated as interchangeable, and first-transfer results should be separated from cumulative live birth.

ASRM supports considering freeze-only treatment for high ovarian response or elevated estradiol when OHSS risk is substantial. This is a safety indication, not proof that routine freezing improves every patient’s chance of a baby.

The 2026 natural-versus-programmed trial concerns preparation for frozen transfer in ovulatory women. Its findings should not be described as a fresh-versus-frozen comparison or applied automatically to irregular ovulation.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to ask why a strategy is being recommended and which outcome matters to you. Your fertility team should relate the evidence to your own cycle and explain reasonable alternatives.

When to seek help

Do not change prescribed fertility medicines on your own. Seek prompt clinic advice for pain, bloating, vomiting, faintness or bleeding, and emergency care for breathing difficulty, chest pain, dehydration with reduced urine, swelling, one-sided lower abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Separate using a stored embryo from choosing freeze-all for an entire collection.
  • Compare live birth over the whole strategy, not just a positive test or a per-transfer rate.
  • OHSS risk and IVF prognosis can change which approach is preferable.
  • Natural and programmed frozen-transfer preparation have different trade-offs.
  • Ask for the clinical reason, full costs, timetable and plan if transfer is postponed.

Frequently asked questions

Does age matter when choosing fresh or frozen transfer?

Yes, but use the correct age history: the age of the egg provider at collection matters for the embryo’s potential, while the health of the person carrying the pregnancy matters at transfer. Age alone does not identify one universally better strategy.

Is a frozen transfer always cheaper?

No. Using an embryo already stored can avoid another egg collection, but electively freezing all embryos adds procedures and delay compared with a fresh-first plan. Compare complete estimates, including storage, monitoring, medicines and cancellation.

Which is better, fresh or frozen transfer?

Neither is best for everyone. Freezing can reduce OHSS risk in high responders, while evidence in low-prognosis patients can favour a fresh-first approach. Ask which patient group and outcome support your clinic’s recommendation.

What is the basic difference between fresh and frozen transfer?

Fresh transfer uses an embryo from the current collection without first freezing it. Frozen transfer uses a stored embryo after warming. Freeze-all deliberately postpones the first transfer from a collection.

Does choosing a fresh transfer prevent later frozen transfers?

No. Suitable embryos remaining after a fresh transfer may be stored and used later. This is why cumulative results from a collection are useful when comparing strategies.

Does every frozen transfer happen without medicines?

No. Preparation may follow ovulation or use a programmed hormone regimen. Even a modified natural cycle can include medicines. Follow the schedule prescribed for your own cycle.

Does PGT-A make freezing automatically worthwhile?

No. PGT-A has a separate indication and limitations. It does not repair embryos or reliably improve the chance of a baby for most IVF patients. Discuss the specific test and expected benefit before combining decisions.

Does freeze-all eliminate OHSS?

No. It is an important risk-reduction measure for selected patients, but early OHSS can still occur after stimulation. Keep monitoring appointments and seek help for concerning symptoms even if no transfer is planned.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
